Boston by the numbers

Where is Boston and how is the city laid out?

Boston is the state capital and the seat of Suffolk County, on the western edge of Boston Harbor. Wikipedia lists the city as settled in 1625 and incorporated as a city on March 19, 1822. It covers 89.61 square miles in total, but only 48.34 of those are land, because 41.27 square miles are water.

The 2020 census counted 675,647 residents, the most of any city in Massachusetts. A good share of the land came from fill. Wikipedia notes that more than two-thirds of inner Boston's modern land area did not exist when the city was founded, and Back Bay is one of the areas built on gravel hauled in by train. That history matters to owners because soil, basements and foundations differ a lot from one block to the next.

The city's Office of Neighborhood Services recognizes 23 neighborhoods, including Allston, Back Bay, Beacon Hill, Charlestown, Dorchester, East Boston, Fenway, Hyde Park, Jamaica Plain, Mattapan, Roslindale, Roxbury, South Boston, the South End and West Roxbury. Each one can have a different mix of triple-deckers, rowhouses, condos and single families, and each is billed through the same city tax system.

What drives the Boston economy?

Health care, higher education, finance and biotechnology carry the Boston economy. Wikipedia describes the city as led by finance, professional and business services, information technology and government, and calls Greater Boston the largest biotechnology hub in the world. It puts the Greater Boston economy at $610 billion.

The 2023 list of top city employers on Wikipedia is mostly hospitals, which tells you where much of the housing demand comes from:

  • Brigham and Women's Hospital
  • Dana-Farber Cancer Institute
  • Massachusetts General Hospital
  • Beth Israel Deaconess Medical Center
  • Boston Children's Hospital
  • Boston Medical Center
  • Boston University School of Medicine
  • The Massachusetts Bay Transportation Authority
  • TIAA
  • Tufts Children's Hospital

Hospitals and universities are tied to specific campuses, so the neighborhoods around them are where a seller is most likely to meet buyers who work nearby.

What does Boston's weather and age of housing mean for a house?

Boston winters are cold and stormy, so roofs, gutters, heating systems and pipes take the most wear. Wikipedia describes a humid climate with warm to hot summers, cold winters and occasional periods of heavy snow, and it notes that areas near the coast often see more rain than snow in winter.

Logan Airport sits only 19 feet above sea level, and the city is bordered by Boston Harbor and the Atlantic. Waterfront and low-lying streets deserve a closer look at basement moisture. Pair that with the 1947 median build year shown above and an older house may be due for roof, wiring or boiler work.

If the repairs are more than you want to take on, selling as-is is one way out. A cash buyer prices the condition in, so you skip the contractor visits.

Who bills and collects Boston property tax?

Two offices share the work: Assessing sets the value and Tax Collection sends and collects the bill. Both sit in City Hall at 1 City Hall Square. Assessing is in Room 301, and the Collector is at Window M-30.

Boston runs on a July 1 to June 30 fiscal year and bills quarterly. The first and second quarter bills are estimates built from last year's value and rate. The real rate shows up on the third quarter bill, which the city says is typically issued in late December.

The Boston Assessing page lists a 2026 rate of $12.40 per $1,000 for residential property and $26.96 for commercial, industrial and personal property. Boston uses a classification system, which lets it charge those two classes different rates. Proposition 2½, passed by voters in 1980, caps how fast the city's total levy can grow, but the city is clear that it does not limit growth in an individual assessment.

How does the Boston residential exemption work?

The residential exemption takes part of a home's value out of taxation if you own it and live in it as your primary residence. Boston says it saved qualified homeowners up to $4,353.74 last fiscal year, and the credit is applied to the third quarter bill in late December.

For FY2027, the city says the application is due by April 1, 2027. A recent home rule petition widened the rules: owners who recorded a deed at the Suffolk County Registry of Deeds and moved in between January 1 and June 30, 2026 may now qualify for the current year. Owners who owned and occupied on January 1, 2026 still qualify.

  • You can claim the exemption on one property only.
  • Filing does not postpone a payment that is due.
  • Other exemptions can stack with it, but taxable value cannot drop below 10 percent of assessed value, with exceptions for some residents with physical ailments or financial hardship.
  • Applications are downloaded from the Boston Property Lookup tool after the December bills go out.

If you are selling, this matters in both directions. A buyer who moves in can apply for the exemption, so a seller should not promise a buyer a tax figure. Ask the Taxpayer Referral and Assistance Center what the current bill looks like.

How do I challenge a Boston assessment?

File an abatement application with the Assessing Department by mail or in person before February 1, 2027 for FY2027. Assessing's direct line is 617-635-4288. If the department denies the request, you have three months from its decision to appeal to the Appellate Tax Board at 100 Cambridge Street, 2nd Floor, Suite 200, Boston, MA 02114, phone 617-727-3100.

Ask the Collector how an open abatement affects the bill you currently owe. If you own a condo with a deeded parking space, check for two bills. Boston says a condo unit appears as class CD and the parking space as class CP, and both must be paid because together they equal the full property value.

What does selling a Boston house involve at the state level?

Massachusetts treats a house sale as a recorded transaction that usually involves a real estate attorney. The state Trial Court Law Libraries say attorneys are a regular part of buying and selling by law and by practice, and that the deed to 80 to 90 percent of properties is filed as recorded land at the county Registry of Deeds. Boston deeds go to the Suffolk County registry.

Three state rules show up for most sellers:

  • Deeds excise. The Department of Revenue lists the deeds tax as $2.28 per $500 of the sales price, less any mortgage assumed.
  • Smoke and CO certificate. A seller needs a certificate of compliance from the local fire department showing the alarms meet requirements for a sale. The fire department charges a fee.
  • Inspection waivers. State regulation 760 CMR 74 says sellers of certain residential properties will not condition an offer on a waiver of the home inspection.

A cash sale keeps all three in place. What changes is who is waiting on repairs and financing.

What happens to unpaid Boston property tax when I sell?

Unpaid tax can be settled from the sale proceeds at closing, which lowers what you take home. Ask the city for the exact amount owed before you sign. For current-year questions call 617-635-4287, and for earlier years call the Collector at 617-635-4131.

If the property was tied up in a probate or inherited situation, tax questions can run alongside other deadlines. The Massachusetts estate tax and the capital gains rules are covered on our other state pages, and the homestead page covers the separate state homestead protection.

More questions about Boston, MA Property Tax Guide

What is the Boston residential property tax rate?

Boston lists a 2026 residential rate of $12.40 per $1,000 of assessed value. The commercial, industrial and personal property rate is $26.96 per $1,000. The final rate for a fiscal year appears on the third quarter bill.

When are Boston property tax abatement applications due?

For fiscal year 2027, the deadline is February 1, 2027. You file with the Assessing Department by mail or in person. If it is denied, you have three months from the decision to appeal to the Appellate Tax Board.

Can I get Boston's residential exemption if I just bought my home?

Possibly. Boston says owners who recorded a deed at the Suffolk County Registry of Deeds and occupied the home between January 1 and June 30, 2026 may qualify for FY2027. The application is due April 1, 2027.

Do I have to pay tax on a condo parking space in Boston?

Yes, if you receive a separate bill. Boston labels the unit class CD and the parking space class CP, and both bills must be paid because together they make up the full property value.

Can I sell a Boston house with unpaid property tax?

Yes, in general. The unpaid amount can be settled from the proceeds at closing. Ask the city for the exact amount owed through the Taxpayer Referral and Assistance Center at 617-635-4287.

Cambridge by the numbers

Where is Cambridge, MA and how big is it?

Cambridge sits in Middlesex County directly across the Charles River from Boston. It covers 7.10 square miles in total, 6.40 of them land, and the 2020 census counted 118,403 residents, which Wikipedia ranks fourth in Massachusetts behind Boston, Worcester and Springfield.

The area was settled in 1630, incorporated in 1636 and became a city in 1846. ZIP codes run from 02138 to 02142. The city runs under a council-manager form of government, so day-to-day operations, including the assessing and finance offices that handle your tax bill, report to a city manager.

The small footprint packs people in. Wikipedia gives a density of 18,510.7 people per square mile, so a Cambridge house usually has close neighbors, and each parcel is valued and taxed on its own record.

What are the squares and neighborhoods of Cambridge?

Cambridge is called the City of Squares because its commercial districts are major street intersections, and each square works as a neighborhood center. Wikipedia names these among others:

  • Kendall Square, at Broadway, Main Street and Third Street, next to MIT and the Kendall/MIT Red Line station.
  • Harvard Square, with Cambridge Common close by and the Baldwin neighborhood north of Harvard.
  • Porter Square, a mile up Massachusetts Avenue, with a Red Line stop and a commuter rail stop.
  • Inman Square, at Cambridge and Hampshire Streets in Mid-Cambridge.
  • Lechmere Square, by the CambridgeSide Galleria and the Green Line.
  • Central Square, plus East Cambridge, Cambridgeport and North Cambridge.

The Red Line also links Cambridge squares to the Somerville border, where Inman and Porter sit very close to the city line.

What drives the Cambridge economy?

Universities, biotech and research firms carry the economy. Harvard, founded in 1636, is the oldest institution of higher learning in the United States, and MIT has a 168-acre campus in the city. Wikipedia reports that in 2022 Cambridge was home to more than 250 biotech companies, with over 120 inside the Kendall Square ZIP code.

Technology companies such as Google, IBM Research, Microsoft Research and Philips Research maintain offices there, and nonprofits and think tanks cluster near the universities. In the nineteenth century the largest employer was the New England Glass Company, founded in 1818, which shows how much the base has changed.

Cambridge also has a rental history that still affects landlord-sellers. Wikipedia says rent control ended in Massachusetts in 1994, and that Cambridge's version had been unusually strict.

How does Cambridge's climate affect a house?

Cambridge has four distinct seasons, so heating systems, roofs and windows get the heaviest use. Wikipedia classifies the climate as hot-summer humid continental, with warm to hot summers, cool and rainy spring and fall, and cold, gray winters with occasional snowstorms. The average January temperature is 26.6 degrees Fahrenheit.

The city's elevation is 39 feet and it borders the Charles River on one side. Cambridge also controls two areas outside its limits for its water supply, including the Hobbs Brook and Stony Brook watersheds, which tells you the municipal water system is a city-run service. That matters at closing, because water and sewer charges can end up on the tax bill, as the next section explains.

Who bills Cambridge property tax and when is it due?

Assessing values the property and the Finance Department bills and collects. Cambridge bills twice a year. For FY2027 the first-half bill was issued October 19, 2026 and is due November 18, 2026, and the city's page lists the FY2027 rates as $6.95 per $1,000 residential and $16.99 per $1,000 commercial and industrial.

The Assessing page adds a heads-up for owners: if your FY2027 first-half bill includes a water and sewer lien, contact the Finance Department at 617-349-4220. That office also handles municipal lien certificates and online payments.

ItemCambridge says
FY2027 residential rate$6.95 per $1,000
FY2027 commercial and industrial rate$16.99 per $1,000
First-half bill issuedOctober 19, 2026
First-half bill dueNovember 18, 2026
Abatement periodOctober 19 to November 18, 2026
Residential exemption applicationApril 1, 2027
Assessing phone617-349-4343
Finance phone617-349-4220

How do I apply for the Cambridge residential exemption?

Apply by April 1 of the fiscal year, and for FY2027 that date is April 1, 2027. The exemption removes part of the value of an owner-occupied home from taxation, and Cambridge uses January 1 to test the ownership and occupancy rules. For FY2027 the test date is January 1, 2026.

New owners should read this carefully. If you bought a Cambridge property and the exemption carried over from the previous owner, you must qualify on your own in order to keep it into the next fiscal year. You submit the application through the city's online portal, which requires a Viewpoint account, or you can ask Assessing for a paper form at 617-349-4343.

  • Other personal exemptions can be combined with it, but taxable value cannot fall below 10 percent of assessed value.
  • Income-related exemptions need a copy of the 2025 income tax return.
  • Assessing's office is at 795 Massachusetts Avenue, Ground Floor, open Monday 8:30 to 8, Tuesday to Thursday 8:30 to 5, and Friday 8:30 to noon.

When you sell, the buyer is the one who needs to qualify. Do not tell a buyer the exemption will transfer.

How does a Cambridge abatement work, and how urgent is it?

The Cambridge abatement window for FY2027 runs from October 19 to November 18, 2026, which is the same date the first-half bill is due. Assessing says assessed values follow full and fair cash value, meaning 100 percent of fair market value, and it uses cost, income and market approaches to reach that figure.

To dispute a value, file with Assessing by mail or in person and be ready to show recent comparable sales. Assessing also held online help sessions during the abatement period, and staff can be reached at 617-349-4343 or assessors@cambridgema.gov. If the result is not what you want, the next level is the Appellate Tax Board, and the clock there is three months from the decision.

Ask Assessing how a pending request affects the bill you owe before you hold back any payment.

What else should a Cambridge seller know about closing?

Cambridge sellers deal with the same state steps as the rest of Massachusetts. The Trial Court Law Libraries say attorneys are a regular part of buying and selling by law and by practice, and the Department of Revenue lists the deeds excise at $2.28 per $500 of the sales price. Cambridge deeds are recorded at the Registry of Deeds, and state land records can be searched at masslandrecords.com.

A seller also needs a certificate of compliance from the local fire department showing the smoke and carbon monoxide alarms meet the sale requirements, and the fire department charges a fee. Ask the Finance Department for a municipal lien certificate so you know exactly what is owed on the tax and any water or sewer lien before you set a closing date.

More questions about Cambridge, MA Property Tax Guide

What is the Cambridge residential property tax rate for FY2027?

The FY2027 residential rate is $6.95 per $1,000 of assessed value, and the commercial and industrial rate is $16.99 per $1,000. The city lists both on its FY27 Property Tax Information page.

When is the first-half Cambridge tax bill due?

The first-half FY2027 real estate bill was issued October 19, 2026 and is due November 18, 2026. Cambridge bills twice a year. The second-half date was not clear on the page we opened, so check with the Finance Department.

What is the deadline for a Cambridge abatement in FY2027?

The abatement period runs October 19 to November 18, 2026. Contact the Assessing Department at 617-349-4343 right away if you plan to file.

Will the residential exemption transfer to the buyer of my Cambridge house?

No, the buyer has to qualify on their own. Cambridge says a new owner who inherited the exemption must still qualify in order to continue receiving it in the next fiscal year.

How do I find out what is owed before selling a Cambridge house?

Request a municipal lien certificate from the Finance Department at 617-349-4220. The Assessing page directs questions about those certificates and online payments to that office.

Last updated November 14, 2026.

Who bills what in Quincy

  • Quincy Assessors Office / Board of Assessors handles assessment.

Due dates

Quarterly: Q1 due Aug 1 and Q2 due Nov 1 (preliminary, about 50% of prior-year tax); Q3 due Feb 1 and Q4 due May 1 (actual bills).. See the official page.

Challenging your assessment

File an abatement between January 1 and February 1 (next Monday if Feb 1 falls on a weekend); late filings must be denied by law; appeal to ATB within 3 months of assessors' action per state guide.. See the official page.

Quincy by the numbers

Who bills and collects property tax in Quincy?

Quincy splits the work between two city offices. The Assessors' Office sets values, and the Treasurer-Collector sends the bills and takes payment.

The Quincy Assessors describe their job as appraising roughly 27,000 parcels, including residential, commercial, industrial and utility property. They also handle abatement and exemption requests, defend values before the state Appellate Tax Board, and report every sale in the city to the Massachusetts Department of Revenue. The office sits at 1305 Hancock Street, 1st Floor, and answers at (617) 376-1170 on weekdays from 8:30 AM to 4:30 PM.

The yearly tax rate comes from a budget set by the Mayor and City Council. After a classification hearing in the Council Chamber, the council votes the rates, and the Assessors then commit the total to the Treasurer-Collector. A homeowner who disagrees with a bill therefore has two different conversations: value questions go to the Assessors, payment questions go to the collector.

When are Quincy real estate taxes due?

Quincy bills quarterly, with payments due on August 1, November 1, February 1 and May 1 of each fiscal year.

The first two bills are preliminary. Together they come to about half of the prior year's total tax, split into two equal payments. The third and fourth bills carry the new assessed value and the new rate, and they subtract what you already paid. The new value first appears on the third quarter bill, which goes out in January.

BillDue dateWhat it reflects
Quarter 1August 1Preliminary, half of the prior-year total split in two
Quarter 2November 1Preliminary, second half of that amount
Quarter 3February 1Actual bill with new value and rate
Quarter 4May 1Final installment of the actual bill

For a seller, the practical point is timing. A house listed in early spring may already have three quarters of the year's bills in play, and the amount still owed at closing depends on which installments have been paid.

What is the Quincy property tax rate?

Quincy's residential rate for fiscal year 2026 is $11.78 per $1,000 of assessed value, and the commercial rate is $23.53 per $1,000.

Fiscal yearResidential rateCommercial rate
2024$11.27$22.45
2025$11.53$23.01
2026$11.78$23.53

These figures come from the city's tax rates page. To see what they mean on paper, multiply the assessed value by the rate and divide by 1,000. A home assessed at $600,000 would work out to $7,068 at the fiscal 2026 residential rate, before any exemption. That is simple arithmetic for illustration, not a bill, so check your own assessment and bill.

How do you appeal a Quincy assessment?

You start with an abatement application to the Assessors, and the deadline is usually February 1 in a city that bills quarterly.

The Massachusetts Appellate Tax Board explains the process in its guide to real estate tax appeals. The steps below follow that guide.

  • Pay each installment on time. Timely payment is a jurisdictional requirement, with narrow exceptions such as a tax of $5,000 or less.
  • File the abatement application on the approved form on or before the due date of the first installment of the actual bill.
  • The Assessors have three months to act. If they do nothing, the application is deemed denied after three calendar months.
  • If you still disagree, file with the Appellate Tax Board within three months of the Assessors' action or of the deemed denial.

The board starts from the premise that the assessment is valid, so the owner carries the burden of showing the fair cash value is lower. Recent sales of similar nearby homes, in similar condition, are the usual evidence. Complaining that taxes went up is not enough.

Which exemptions can lower a Quincy tax bill?

Quincy offers statutory exemptions for several groups, and each one has to be applied for every year. For fiscal year 2027 the filing deadline is April 1, 2027.

  • Senior citizens, with separate applications for ages 65 and up and ages 70 and up
  • Legally blind residents
  • Surviving spouses, and minor children of a deceased parent
  • Surviving spouses or minor children of police officers and firefighters
  • Disabled veterans, including those with at least a 10 percent service-related disability

At a minimum, applicants must be domiciled in Quincy. The Assessors also publish a tax deferral explanation for owners who qualify. Details and forms are on the exemption programs page.

If you are selling because of a health change or a death in the family, ask the Assessors whether an exemption you hold affects the final bill. It can change what a closing agent pays out.

What happens if Quincy property tax goes unpaid?

Unpaid property tax becomes a lien automatically, and over time the city can record a tax taking and a private party can pursue foreclosure in Land Court.

The Massachusetts Land Court's tax lien foreclosure overview lays out the general path.

  1. Once a tax or water and sewer bill is unpaid for 30 days, the city can send a demand to the last known address.
  2. If payment is not made within 14 days of the demand, the city can record a tax taking at the Registry of Deeds.
  3. A private party can end up holding the tax title, for example through a bundled sale or an auction.
  4. Six or twelve months after the taking or sale, depending on the date, the holder can file a complaint in Land Court.
  5. The owner can answer, ask for a hearing, and redeem by paying all taxes, interest and fees before a final judgment of foreclosure.

Redemption stays possible until the court enters judgment. That window is the reason many owners in arrears choose to sell: a sale closing can pay the lien off from proceeds, and the owner keeps whatever equity is left.

Where is Quincy and how is it laid out?

Quincy is a city of about 101,636 residents (2020 census) in Norfolk County, directly south of Boston, and the largest city in its county.

It covers 26.9 square miles, and 37.6 percent of that is water, because Quincy Bay and the Neponset and Fore Rivers shape its edges. Roughly 23 percent of the land is the Blue Hills Reservation, a state park that takes up the southwest and holds the city's high point, Chickatawbut Hill at 517 feet. Wollaston Beach is the largest Boston Harbor beach.

Quincy factDetail
2020 population101,636
Total area26.9 square miles, 37.6 percent water
Settled / city status1625 / 1888
Share of land in Blue Hills ReservationAbout 23 percent
Red Line stationsNorth Quincy, Wollaston, Quincy Center, Quincy Adams
Housing units (2020)51,156

The data is from Wikipedia's Quincy article, which cites the Census Bureau.

Which Quincy neighborhoods matter when you sell?

Quincy has more than a dozen named neighborhoods, and a house on a peninsula faces different questions than one near Quincy Center.

  • Squantum, Houghs Neck and Adams Shore are coastal, mostly peninsular areas that began as summer communities and are now year-round homes.
  • Wollaston and North Quincy are dense residential and commercial areas on the Red Line, along Hancock Street and Quincy Shore Drive.
  • Quincy Center holds City Hall, the library and the historic core.
  • Quincy Point includes the Fore River Shipyard site, and Marina Bay was built on the former Naval Air Station Squantum.
  • West Quincy sits beside Interstate 93 and the old granite quarries.

Older stock is common, and the city sits on a coast with a long industrial past. An owner of an older house near the water should expect a buyer to ask about the heating system, the roof and the basement.

How did Quincy's economy develop?

Quincy grew on granite and shipbuilding, then shifted to offices and services.

The Granite Railway, built in 1826 to haul stone toward the Bunker Hill Monument, is called the first commercial railroad in the United States. The Fore River Shipyard built famous warships from the 1880s on. Today the city hosts the headquarters of Stop & Shop, Arbella Insurance Group and Boston Financial Data Services, and offices of State Street, Blue Cross Blue Shield of Massachusetts and Boston Scientific.

That mix matters for sellers because it supports commuter demand tied to the Red Line and Interstate 93, which runs through West Quincy toward Boston. Route 3A and Route 3 reach the rest of the South Shore.

What should a Quincy seller know about closing costs and paperwork?

A Quincy sale involves a deed excise tax, a smoke and carbon monoxide certificate, and payoff of any tax owed.

  • The Norfolk County Registry of Deeds charges a deed excise tax of $2.28 per $500 of the stated consideration. Its fee schedule gives an example: a $155,000 deed owes $706.80.
  • The same schedule lists a $156 recording fee for a deed in recorded land.
  • A sale of a one or two family home needs a certificate of compliance from the local fire department showing that smoke and carbon monoxide alarms meet state requirements. The state's guidance says to call the fire department as soon as you have a closing date.

Ask the Quincy Assessors and Treasurer-Collector for the current balance, because the closing agent needs an exact payoff. We could not open the collector's page, so check with that office for lien certificate timing and fees.

More questions about Quincy, MA Property Tax Guide

How often is Quincy property tax billed?

Quarterly. Bills are due August 1, November 1, February 1 and May 1. The first two are preliminary and total about half of the prior year's tax.

What is Quincy's residential tax rate?

The city lists $11.78 per $1,000 of assessed value for fiscal year 2026. The commercial rate is $23.53 per $1,000.

Can I sell my Quincy house if I owe back property tax?

Yes. Unpaid tax is a lien on the property, and a sale can pay it from the proceeds at closing. Get a written payoff figure from the city before the closing date.

What is the deadline to file for a Quincy property tax exemption?

Applications for fiscal year 2027 are due on or before April 1, 2027, and an exemption application must be filed every year. Applicants must be domiciled in Quincy.

How long do I have to challenge my Quincy assessment?

The abatement application is generally due February 1. After the Assessors act, you have three months to appeal to the Appellate Tax Board.

Does a Quincy house need an inspection before sale?

State rules require a smoke and carbon monoxide certificate of compliance from the local fire department for a one or two family home. Call the department once you have a closing date.

Newton by the numbers

Where is Newton and how is it laid out?

Newton is a city in Middlesex County, about 8 miles west of downtown Boston, made up of thirteen villages rather than one center. Wikipedia's Newton entry lists them: Auburndale, Chestnut Hill, Newton Centre, Newton Corner, Newton Highlands, Newton Lower Falls, Newton Upper Falls, Newtonville, Nonantum, Oak Hill, Thompsonville, Waban and West Newton.

The city borders Boston's Brighton and West Roxbury neighborhoods, Brookline, Watertown, Waltham, Weston, Wellesley and Needham. It covers about 18 square miles, and the Charles River runs along its north and west sides. Seven hills shape the terrain, among them Nonantum Hill, Waban Hill, Chestnut Hill and Mount Ida.

For a homeowner, the village matters more than the city name. Your village affects your ZIP code (Wikipedia lists eleven ZIP codes for Newton), your commute and the kind of house on your street, but it does not change who bills your tax. That is the city's Assessing and Treasury offices, described below.

How did Newton become a city?

The area was first part of Cambridge, which was settled in 1630, and English settlement of what is now Newton began in 1639. It was incorporated as a separate town on December 15, 1681, renamed Newtown in 1691 and then Newton in 1766. It became a city on January 5, 1874.

Water power at Newton Upper Falls and Newton Lower Falls drew small mills that made snuff, chocolate, glue and paper. Wikipedia also notes the Stanley Motor Carriage Company, maker of the Stanley Steamer, was based there from 1902. The railroad reached West Newton in 1834, and the entry describes Newton as one of the earliest commuter suburbs in North America.

That history is why Newton's housing stock is so mixed in age. Streetcar lines and then cars brought new waves of building in the late nineteenth century and the 1920s, and the entry says the whole city became more densely settled in the 1950s.

Who bills and who assesses property tax in Newton?

Newton's Assessing office sets values and handles abatements and exemptions, while the Treasury Department bills and collects. The city's own page says so directly: Assessing determines property values and administers abatements, exemptions and excise adjustments, and Treasury/Collector bills and collects real estate tax.

OfficeWhat it handlesContact on the city site
AssessingValues, abatements, exemptions, tax mailing addressCity Hall, Room 111, 1000 Commonwealth Avenue, Newton Centre, MA 02459. 617-796-1160, assessing@newtonma.gov. Monday to Friday, 8:30 a.m. to 5:00 p.m.
TreasuryPayments, balances, duplicate bills, refunds, municipal lien certificates, tax title617-796-1330, treasury@newtonma.gov

Use the right door. A question about why your value went up goes to Assessing. A question about whether last quarter's payment posted goes to Treasury.

What is Newton's current tax rate?

For fiscal year 2026 the certified rates are $9.69 per $1,000 of assessed value for residential property and $18.06 per $1,000 for commercial, industrial and personal property. Newton's Assessing page shows those figures as the latest certified rates.

The math is simple. A home assessed at $1,000,000 would carry an annual residential levy of $9,690 at $9.69 per $1,000, before any exemption. That example is an illustration of the rate, not a statement about any particular house, and your bill may differ because of exemptions or abatements.

  • Rates are set each fiscal year, so a sale next year will use a different number.
  • The rate multiplies your assessed value, which is why an abatement based on value matters.
  • Look up your parcel in the city's Assessor's Database and map to see your own assessed value.

When is Newton property tax due?

Quarterly, on the first business day of August, November, February and May. Newton's Treasury page lists those installments under its key billing schedules.

Because the due date for the first installment also sets the abatement clock, the dates matter beyond just paying. The state's Appellate Tax Board guide explains that an abatement application must be filed with assessors on or before the due date of the first installment of the actual tax bill, and generally that date is February 1 in quarterly billing communities. The face of your tax bill should show the exact dates.

  • August 1 and November 1: first two installments of the fiscal year.
  • February 1 and May 1: the final two installments.
  • Motor vehicle excise bills are due within 30 days of issue, and utility bills are issued quarterly and due within 30 days of the bill date.

How do you challenge a Newton assessment?

File an abatement application with Newton's Assessing office on time, and pay your tax installments on time. The Appellate Tax Board guide lists three jurisdictional requirements: payment of the tax by the due dates, timely filing of the abatement application on the approved form, and timely filing of any appeal with the Board.

Assessors have three months to act. If they do nothing, the application is deemed denied after three calendar months. A taxpayer then has three months from the date of action or deemed denial to appeal to the Appellate Tax Board.

The standard of proof is on you. The guide says an assessment is presumed valid, and valuation is as of January 1 before the fiscal year, so a bill for fiscal year 2025 reflects a January 1, 2024 date. Comparable sales of similar nearby homes are the usual evidence.

  • Pay every installment by its due date, even while an abatement is pending.
  • File the form with Assessing before the deadline printed on your bill.
  • Collect photos, your property record card and sales of similar homes.

Some exceptions to the payment rule exist for limited cases, so read the guide before deciding to skip a payment.

What exemptions and tax assistance does Newton offer?

Newton lists exemption, deferral, work-off and assistance programs for eligible taxpayers. Its Assessing page says applications for the next fiscal year, FY2027, are available and exemption applications are due on or before April 1, 2027.

The page does not list eligibility terms in the text we opened, so ask Assessing which program fits your age, income or status. If you are selling, ask whether any exemption or deferral on the property will affect your closing payoff. Your closing attorney should ask for any payoff figure.

What happens with Newton property tax when you sell?

Treasury is the office to ask about any balance before a sale. Newton's Treasury page points to a service for requesting a municipal lien certificate and to information about tax title, redemptions and municipal lien releases.

If your tax is behind, ask Treasury what you owe and ask your attorney how it will be paid at closing. Ask Treasury how tax title and redemption work if your account is far behind, and start that conversation early.

  • Request the municipal lien certificate through Treasury.
  • Pay or arrange the balance at closing.
  • Ask Assessing for your current assessment and any open abatement.

Cash Home Buyers buys Newton houses as-is. If you want an offer on a house with taxes due, you can reach out, and any tax payoff is handled through closing.

What shapes demand for Newton houses?

Colleges, a hospital, rail and highways give Newton steady housing demand. Wikipedia names Boston College and Newton-Wellesley Hospital as the largest employers, and the colleges and universities located in the city include Boston College, Lasell University, Hebrew College and William James College.

Transit is a draw. The MBTA Green Line D branch runs through the center of the city, the B branch ends at Boston College, and the Worcester commuter rail serves the northern villages. The Massachusetts Turnpike and Route 9 run east and west, and Route 128 clips the western edge. Public education is provided by Newton Public Schools, with Newton North High School and Newton South High School.

Wikipedia puts annual precipitation at 53.59 inches, a record low of minus 21 degrees in February 1934 and a record high of 101 in August 1975. A house with an aging roof or heating system faces that weather every year, which buyers tend to ask about.

More questions about Newton, MA Property Tax Guide

Who sends my Newton property tax bill?

The city's Treasury Department bills and collects the tax, while Assessing sets the value. Treasury can be reached at 617-796-1330.

When are Newton property taxes due?

Quarterly, on the first business day of August, November, February and May, according to the Treasury page.

What is the Newton residential tax rate?

The certified FY2026 rate is $9.69 per $1,000 of assessed value for residential property and $18.06 for commercial, industrial and personal property.

What is the abatement deadline in Newton?

The state guide says an abatement application is due by the first installment due date on the bill, generally February 1 in quarterly billing communities. Check your bill or call Assessing at 617-796-1160 for the exact date.

Can I sell a Newton house with unpaid property tax?

Yes, but ask your closing attorney how the balance will be paid. Treasury offers a municipal lien certificate request and can tell you what you owe.

What is the deadline for FY2027 exemption applications?

Newton's Assessing page says exemption applications are due on or before April 1, 2027.
